title: Tansyspoon and the Moonpetal Mystery
markdown:
Mist swirled around the mountaintops like a soft grey scarf. Ancient towers, mossy, forgotten by soldiers, stood against the sky. Paths wound, some carved by old feet, others by the scamper of forest creatures. This was goblin country, and among them lived Tansyspoon, who loved his garden more than anything.

He was not like other goblins. He did not collect shiny stones or play silly tricks. His treasures were sage leaves, the cheerful smell of thyme, and the special glow of his moonpetal herb, star of the garden, his pride. Today his whiskers twitched. Big clumsy footprints in the beds—not little goblin prints, giant ones, right by the prize-winning moonpetal.

A thyme plant leaned, offended. Sage leaves wore muddy thumbprints that were not thumbs. The moonpetal still glowed, but the soil around it was a mess of heels.

“Oh, fiddle-dee-dee!” Glasses sliding. “Who would stomp on such perfection?”

On his ear, Tinny buzzed: a beetle shining like a green and blue jewel. Usually a happy sound; now a tiny flustered horn.

The Grand Herb Competition was days away. The village excited. Wizard Alder, beard like moonlight and cinnamon, was the judge. Tansyspoon had practised speeches until his voice was a dry whisper, polished his trowel, sorted his seeds. He needed the moonpetal perfect. And now this clumsy giant mess.

“It’s not fair.” Shoulders like wilted flowers. Fluttery knees, tiny scared fireflies. He was a small goblin. What against someone who left such footprints? A troll who forgot how to walk softly.

“Brave heart,” he told himself, words from an old stone in the Whispering Grove. “Cleverness is better than size.” Chest puffed like a proud puffball. He had to find who did this. Save the moonpetal.

Tinny buzzed a strong steady beat, a tiny drum of support.

The muddy prints led toward the Whispering Woods: confusing paths, echoes that played tricks. “Come on, Tinny. We’re going on an adventure.”

Sturdy boots, small trowel, Tinny clinging like a buzzing badge of courage. He packed a pinch of dried sage in a twist of paper, because a garden goblin did not leave home empty-handed.

In the square, colourful banners. Alder watched preparations. This year’s competition was a friendly contest with Witch Willowisp, who grew herbs so powerful they could sing opera. Alder liked herbs that healed and brought happy dreams. Excitement buzzed, though Willowisp was known for being very competitive.

A child waved a paper moonpetal. Tansyspoon did not wave back. He was already following mud.

Deeper in the woods, old trees close as sleeping giants’ arms. Path narrow, moss-slick. “Whoa!” Tansyspoon slid. Tinny buzzed like a tiny siren, steering them from prickly bushes. “Good save, Tinny!” Scrambling up. Knees still tingling.

He found a print pressed into fern. Another. Then a gap, as if the walker had leapt, or flown, or simply not cared about being followed.

A cave where every sound bounced. “Hello?” “Hello! Hello! Lo! Llo!” Echoes teased, making him smaller. Tinny a steady tiny anchor. Footprints playing hide-and-seek. Just as he felt like giving up, Tinny darted toward a hidden opening behind ivy. “That way?” He squeezed through. The trowel scraped stone. He apologised to the stone, which was a garden habit and not, strictly, useful.

A sunny clearing. Hunched over bright glow-wort: Witch Willowisp, face hidden by a wide hat. Tansyspoon’s mouth fell open. She was collecting herbs, and not quietly. Tall. Big boots making the same heavy thuds as the garden prints. She tried to tiptoe; cloak snagged; steps as subtle as a dragon hiding behind a dandelion.

“That dragon,” he whispered to Tinny, a small smile, “is trying to be sneaky. It’s not her best trick.”

Willowisp’s head shot up. Mischief, then annoyance. Caught. Now a race.

She ran, leaves rustling. “Hey!” Anger made him forget fear. He and Tinny followed, small figures after long strides.

Willowisp waved a hand: shimmering dust, a fake wall of moss. Tansyspoon faltered, heart in his throat. “It’s not real, Tinny!” Shaky. Tinny flew straight through the illusion, pulling him. “Clever you!” Amazed. The fake moss smelled of nothing. Real moss always smelled of wet wood and patience.

Then thick swirling mist, overripe berries and damp socks. He coughed, eyes watering, stumbled. Tinny a faint shining blur. “Where are you going?” Muffled.

He tripped over a thick root that seemed to reach just for him, tumbled. When the mist cleared he was back near the woods’ edge, looking toward the village. Walking proudly toward the judging stand: Willowisp, a beautiful glowing herb in her hand. It looked exactly like his moonpetal.

Heart sank like a pebble in a well. Nurtured so carefully, gone. He had followed, been brave, not enough. Stolen best chance. Small again, a ladybug facing a herd.

He walked away from the village path to a high hill over a wide dark lake. Deep blue sky, stars like scattered diamonds. The lake a perfect mirror. Beautiful, peaceful; he felt only an empty ache. Cool rock, head in hands. A little goblin who could not even protect his garden. Willowisp winning made the loss worse.

Tinny buzzed softly, soothing. Landed on his hand, tapped a tiny leg: friendship. Tansyspoon looked at his beetle, then the lake. He remembered herbs, not just moonpetal: tiny seeds, watering, sun, dew. The special magic of the whole garden, each herb a story. The competition was not only one plant. Knowledge. Passion. Effort.

He stood, a spark growing to a steady flame. Brushed smudged trousers. “You’re right, Tinny.” Clear on the night air. “She has the moonpetal. I have the knowledge. And other herbs. Herbs with their own special powers.”

From his pocket he took the twist of sage. It was not a prize. It smelled like home anyway. He put it back and went for glimmerleaf, which grew at the garden’s shy edge, silver even in the dark.

Back to the village, steps quickening. Willowisp already at the stand, magnificent herb high: Tansyspoon’s moonpetal, even more beautiful under village lights. Alder looked at it, thoughtful, amused.

Then Tansyspoon arrived. Not the prized moonpetal: a small simple sprig of glimmerleaf. Chin high. Quiet confidence. “Honourable Wizard Alder. You seek the best herb. Witch Willowisp’s herb is indeed my moonpetal. I grew it carefully. It is beautiful. But its magic is gentle. Sweet dreams, tired hearts. Lovely. Its true strength is quiet comfort, a soft song for the soul.”

He held up glimmerleaf, silvery leaves catching light. “This does not glow as brightly. Its scent chases shadows and whispers of doubt. Brewed, it can give courage to the shyest creature.” A sprig to Alder. The wizard inhaled, eyes widening with delight. “It helped me find my own courage,” Tansyspoon admitted, shy smile.

Willowisp scoffed, dry leaves. “Glimmerleaf? No match. Practically a weed.”

Alder beamed, took the sprig carefully. “My dear Willowisp, your moonpetal is splendid, a sign of Tansyspoon’s skill. But he is right. True magic isn’t always the loudest or brightest. This glimmerleaf has a quiet strong charm. Strength. Courage from within. Like our mountain folk, small but mighty.” Twinkling eyes. “For bravery, honesty, and showing that cleverness can grow in the smallest hearts: this year’s Grand Herb Competition winner.”

Applause. Willowisp, surprised, a small nod. Tansyspoon accepted the green ribbon against his tunic. Tinny buzzed a happy song. Later he would replant. The moonpetal would grow again. The garden, footprints and all, still knew his name.
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for independent readers
